title: Sorted List Turned on a Ring
statement:
Someone took an array sorted in non-decreasing order (duplicates allowed) and maybe rotated it: they moved some number of elements, possibly zero, from the front to the back, keeping their order.

Given the result nums, return true if it could have been produced that way, and false otherwise. A rotation by zero counts, so an already sorted array returns true.

examples.why: It is [1, 2, 5, 6, 8, 8] with the first three moved to the back.
There is only one drop inside the array (4 → 1), but going around the ring from 5 back to 3 is a second drop.
Rotate [1, 2, 2, 2]. Equal neighbours are not drops.

hints: In a sorted array, how many times does a value drop compared to the one before it?
Rotation cuts the sorted array in one place. Count the places where nums[i] > nums[i + 1], treating the array as a ring.
Compare each element with the next one, and the last with the first. At most one drop means true.

explain.intuition:
Picture the array as a ring. A sorted array read around the ring goes up (or stays flat) all the way, and then drops exactly once, where the largest value wraps back to the smallest. Rotating it only changes where you start reading. It does not add or remove any drop.

So count the drops around the ring, including the step from the last element back to the first. Zero or one drop means it is a rotated sorted array. Two or more means no rotation can fix it. Zero happens only when every element is equal.
pitfalls: Forgetting the wrap-around comparison from the last element to the first. [3, 4, 1, 2, 5] has only one inner drop but is not a rotation.
Counting equal neighbours as drops. Duplicates are allowed, so use a strict >.
Requiring exactly one drop. A sorted array with no rotation has one drop at the wrap point, but an all-equal array has zero, and both are valid.

solutions.title: Try every rotation
solutions.idea: For each possible start, check whether reading from there is non-decreasing.

solutions.title: Count drops around the ring
solutions.idea: A rotated sorted array drops at most once when read as a ring.

followups: Return how many positions it was rotated by. What goes wrong when there are duplicates?
Find a target value in such an array in O(log n). Which half can you rule out at each step?
